SK2240 The with expression rewrites every member

A with expression assigns every positional parameter of the record it copies, so it constructs a wholly new value through the copy constructor and reads as a copy of the old one.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floorC# 9.0
Since2.0

Why

p with { X = a, Y = b } on a record Point(int X, int Y) is new Point(a, b) spelled longer: nothing of p survives it. The cost is not the ceremony, it is what happens next — add a member to the record and the with silently starts carrying that member across from p, which is the one value the author had already decided not to keep. The constructor call cannot do that: adding a parameter is a compile error at every call site, which is the whole point of writing it that way. ⚠ The question is decidable and is asked as a set comparison, not as a shape match: the names assigned by the initializer against the positional parameters of the record's primary constructor. That is why the rule is Semantic — the parameter list is a fact about the symbol, not about the page.

Example

Instead of:

var moved = point with { X = x, Y = y };

Write:

var moved = new Point(x, y);

When it does not fire

⚠ The record's whole instance state must be its positional parameters, and the predicate is `SK1071`'s because the hazard is `SK1071`'s read backwards. with invokes the copy constructor, which copies every field; new T(…) sets only the parameters. Where the record holds anything else — a field, an event, a settable property outside the parameter list, a base record — the rewrite silently drops it, so all of those decline. ⚠ `sealed` is required for the same reason `SK1071` requires it, in the opposite direction: x with { … } returns x's runtime type through the virtual clone and new T(…) returns exactly T, so on an unsealed record holding a derived instance the two forms produce different objects. ⚠ Every positional property must be the auto-property the record synthesized, asked by comparing the property's declaring syntax against the parameter's — they are the same ParameterSyntax for a positional record. ⚠ `IsImplicitlyDeclared` is the obvious test for that and it is the wrong one: it is `false` for a positional record property, because the parameter is where the property is written down. A rule testing it as true would match nothing and pass every negative fixture. ⚠ Disjoint from `SK0230` by construction. SK0230 reports x with { }, an initializer with no assignments; this rule requires an assignment for every positional parameter and a record with at least one, so no with expression can be reported by both. ⚠ Disjoint from `SK1071` by construction, and the guard that makes it so is the one that stops the two rules fixing each other in a loop. SK1071 rewrites new R(x.A, x.B, c) into x with { C = c } — an initializer that sets fewer than all the members, which this rule declines. In the other direction the hazard is real and is guarded explicitly: x with { X = x.X, Y = b } assigns every member and would fix to new T(x.X, b), which is exactly SK1071's shape and would be fixed straight back. Any assignment whose value is the same member read off the same receiver therefore withdraws the finding, and a fixture asserts the round trip terminates. ⚠ The receiver must be a simple local or parameter name. GetPoint() with { X = a, Y = b } rewrites to new Point(a, b), which drops the call entirely — an evaluation the original performed and the replacement does not. ⚠ The fix is not safe and null is the reason. with dereferences its operand, so a null receiver throws a NullReferenceException that new T(…) does not; the rewrite therefore removes a throw, which is a change a person has to look at. It is the same reason SK0230 carries fixIsSafe: false. A named argument, a ref/out argument and an initializer holding a comment or a preprocessor directive all decline. Generated code is excluded.
